::: {.bnr-manual-flag .bnr-manual-flag--methods}
Public Methods Manual
:::

BNR identifies public releases so that users can tell which data and methods produced a result. Figures may be revised when source information improves or a controlled correction is required.

## Why this matters

A value copied from an earlier report or download may not be identical to a
later dashboard value for the same period. The difference may reflect later
records, resolved outcomes, source corrections or a defined method change.

## Types of change

| Change | Example | Effect on comparison |
|--|---|---|
| **Data maturation** | A late record or completed outcome is added | Recent values may change |
| **Correction** | A duplicate or invalid date is resolved | A previous value is replaced through a controlled release |
| **Method revision** | A denominator source or classification rule changes | Although this type of change is rare, the series may require a documented break or recalculation |
| **Presentation change** | Labels or layout improve without changing values | Statistical comparability is unchanged |

## Stable and release-stamped outputs

BNR maintains two current cumulative data files: one for CVD events and one for CVD deaths. These files provide straightforward access to the latest approved data.

BNR also keeps date- and release-stamped versions of each dataset. Reports and other published products identify the specific release used, allowing users to find the exact data behind a result and reproduce it later.

## Release date and data period

The **release date** is when BNR publishes an approved dataset or report. The **data period** is the most recent month, quarter or year included in it. These dates may differ.

This is particularly important for mortality data. Death registration and classification take time, so a release published in 2026 may contain complete data only to 2025 or earlier.

When describing how up to date a result is, use the displayed data period—not the publication date alone.

## Comparing periods

Before deciding that a result has changed over time, check that you are comparing like with like:

1. the same event or measure definition;
2. the same sources and population coverage;
3. the same population denominator and, for age-adjusted rates, the same standard population;
4. similar completeness and reporting delay;
5. the same groups and level of detail; and
6. whether either period has been revised.

::: {.callout-warning title="A change in method can look like a change in health"}
A change in data sources, definitions or coverage can alter a trend even when the underlying health situation has not changed. BNR identifies important changes so that unlike results are not presented as directly comparable.
:::

## What to remember

- Use a release-stamped dataset when you need to reproduce a result.
- Check the data period as well as the publication date.
- Compare results only when their definitions and source coverage are compatible.
- When BNR publishes a revised figure, it replaces the earlier current figure and explains the reason for the change.
